summary: Jesus sits on a mountain and describes the people God's reign calls fortunate: the poor in spirit, mourners, the meek, those hungry for righteousness, the merciful, pure in heart, peacemakers, and persecuted. He names disciples salt and light, affirms the Law and Prophets, then moves from commands to the dispositions and relationships they protect — anger, desire, fidelity, truthful speech, retaliation, and enemy love.
whyItMatters: This is not a preface Matthew expects readers to admire and leave behind. It defines a righteousness enacted from the heart and visible in reconciled, truthful, nonretaliatory love. Jesus speaks with the scriptural authority of a teacher on a mountain while repeatedly claiming, ‘But I tell you.’

context.author: Anonymous Gospel narrator arranging the first major discourse
context.audience: Disciples and crowds within a Jewish scriptural world
context.date: Late-first-century Gospel preserving and arranging earlier teaching
context.setting: A mountain in Galilee as a literary and geographical teaching place
context.literaryForm: Wisdom blessings, prophetic interpretation, legal examples, and memorable hyperbole

keyVerses.text: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.
keyVerses.why: The opening blessing announces divine favor before it issues any command.

keyVerses.text: “Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill.
keyVerses.why: Jesus frames the examples that follow as bringing Scripture to fullness, not discarding it.

keyVerses.text: But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you,
keyVerses.why: The movement reaches its climax in love that imitates the Father's indiscriminate generosity.

questions.question: Does ‘blessed’ mean emotionally happy?
questions.answer: Makarios names someone fortunate or in an enviable position because of God's favor and promised future, even when present feeling is grief or persecution. The form comes from Psalms and wisdom literature. It is a declaration before it is an instruction: God sees people the world overlooks.

questions.question: Does ‘poor in spirit’ make actual poverty irrelevant?
questions.answer: No. Matthew's phrase emphasizes dependence and humility before God, while the Gospel repeatedly addresses material need and wealth. Luke's parallel says simply ‘poor.’ The versions should illuminate rather than cancel each other: Matthew specifies a posture without declaring economic suffering spiritually unimportant.

questions.question: What does ‘fulfill’ the Law and Prophets mean?
questions.answer: Plēroō means fill or bring to completion. In this discourse Jesus confirms Scripture's authority, embodies its aim, and authoritatively exposes the relationships its commands protect. ‘Fulfill’ cannot mean ‘abolish,’ because verse 17 rejects that; neither does it mean every command applies without being interpreted through Jesus's teaching.

questions.question: Is ‘You have heard … but I say’ Jesus correcting Moses?
questions.answer: Some examples quote Scripture; others quote a teaching derived from it. Jesus does not repeatedly say ‘Scripture was wrong.’ He contrasts inherited formulations with his own authoritative demand, moving from minimum legal boundaries toward reconciled relationships, undivided fidelity, transparent truth, relinquished vengeance, and enemy love.

questions.question: What are Raca and Gehenna?
questions.answer: Raca preserves an Aramaic insult roughly like ‘empty-head’; Gehenna comes from the Valley of Hinnom near Jerusalem and had become an image of divine judgment. Jesus escalates from anger to contempt to judgment to show that speech can enact the destruction forbidden by the murder command. The terms are not magic syllables with automatic penalties.

questions.question: Are commands to remove an eye or hand literal self-mutilation?
questions.answer: They are shocking moral hyperbole: remove the source of betrayal with the urgency one would use to save a whole body. Physical mutilation does not remove coveting from the heart, the very level Jesus is addressing. The image must retain its seriousness without becoming a command to injure oneself.

questions.question: Does ‘turn the other cheek’ require remaining in abuse?
questions.answer: The saying renounces personal retaliation and interrupts cycles of humiliation; the surrounding examples relinquish the right to answer coercion in kind. It does not command secrecy, remove the community's duty to protect, or forbid escape and justice. Enemy love names active good and prayer, not permission for an abuser to continue harming.

questions.question: Does ‘perfect’ mean never making a mistake?
questions.answer: Teleios can mean complete, whole, or mature. Here the comparison is the Father's generous love toward good and evil alike. Jesus calls disciples toward an undivided love that does not stop at the boundary of one's group; the sentence is not a vocabulary trick that makes the demand easy, nor a command to neurotic flawlessness.

glossary.def: A wisdom-form declaration beginning ‘blessed’ or ‘fortunate,’ naming those favored by God.
Life aligned with God's will, encompassing justice, mercy, fidelity, devotion, and conduct.
A name derived from Jerusalem's Valley of Hinnom that became an image of divine judgment.
